intro:
Malta, officially the Republic of Malta, is an island country located in the central Mediterranean Sea. It consists of a number of islands, of which Malta and Gozo are the two main ones—south of Italy, east of Tunisia, and north of Libya. Valletta is the country's capital. Malta is the world's tenth-smallest country by area, ninth-most densely populated, and 166th most populated. It consists of a single urban region, because of which it is often described as a city-state. The two official languages are Maltese—recognised as the national language—and English.

The island of Malta has been inhabited since at least 6500 BC, during the Mesolithic period. Its location at the centre of the Mediterranean has historically given it great geostrategic importance, with multiple powers having ruled the islands and shaped its culture and society. Included among these powers the Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Greeks, and Romans in antiquity; the Arabs, Normans, and Aragonese during the Middle Ages; and the Knights Hospitaller, French, and British in the modern era.

Malta came under British rule as a crown colony in the early 19th century and served as the headquarters of the British Mediterranean Fleet. It was sieged by the Axis powers during World War II and was also an Allied base for its area. The country gained independence in 1964, and established its current parliamentary republic in 1974. It has been a member state of the Commonwealth of Nations and the United Nations since its independence, joining the European Union (EU) in 2004 and the eurozone monetary union in 2008. Malta's history of foreign rule and its proximity to both Europe and North Africa have influenced its art, music, cuisine, and architecture. It has close historical and cultural ties to Italy, especially to the island of Sicily, with 66 percent of Maltese people speaking or having significant knowledge of the Italian language. The country was an early centre of Christianity, and Catholicism is the state religion, although the country's constitution guarantees freedom of religion.

Malta is now a developed country with an advanced, high-income economy. It is heavily reliant on tourism, attracting travellers because of its warm climate, recreational areas, and architectural and historical monuments.

sections.Etymology: The English name Malta derives from classical Latin Melita, from Latinised forms of the ancient Greek Melítē (Μελίτη), of uncertain meaning, possibly from the Phoenician Maleth. The name Melítē—shared by the Croatian island Mljet in antiquity—literally means "place of honey" or "place of sweetness", derived from the combining form of méli (μέλι, honey or any similarly sweet thing), and the suffix -ē (-η). The ancient Greeks may have named the island this after Malta's endemic subspecies of bees.
sections.Geography: Malta is an archipelago in the eastern basin of the central Mediterranean Sea, some 80 km (50 mi) from southern Italy across the Malta Channel. Only the three largest islands—Malta, Gozo, and Comino— have permanent residences, though Comino is practically uninhabited. The islands of the archipelago lie on the Malta plateau, a shallow shelf formed from the high points of a land bridge between Sicily and North Africa that became isolated as sea levels rose after the last ice age. The archipelago is located on the African tectonic plate.
sections.Government and politics: Malta is a republic, the parliamentary system and public administration of which are modelled on the Westminster system. The Parliament is made up of the president and the House of Representatives (Maltese: Kamra tad-Deputati). The president is appointed for a five-year term by a simple majority of the House of Representatives. The current president, Myriam Spiteri Debono, was elected on 27 March 2024 by members of Parliament.
sections.Economy:
Malta is classified as an advanced economy by the International Monetary Fund (IMF). It has a large amount of limestone contributing to its economy. Maltese agriculture produces only around 20 percent of its food needs, with limited fresh water supplies in the summer and no domestic energy sources (although there is solar power potential). The economy is dependent on foreign trade, manufacturing (especially electronics and textiles), and tourism. The agriculture is mainly small-scale farms by families who have other jobs.

Film production has also contributed to the Maltese economy. The country's variety of landscapes and destinations has become a significant draw for filmmakers. Films shot on the island include both Gladiator films, Gladiator and Gladiator II, and several episodes of the 1970s British spy drama The Sandbaggers.
sections.Tourism:
Malta is a popular tourist destination, with 1.6 million tourists per year as of 2015, three times more tourists than residents. In 2017, there were over 2.3 million tourists, mainly from Britain, Italy, Australia, and the United States. Tourism contributes around 11.6 percent of Malta's GDP.

In recent years, Malta has advertised itself as a medical tourism destination, and a number of health tourism providers are developing the industry. However, no Maltese hospital has undergone independent international healthcare accreditation. Malta is popular with British medical tourists in particular.
sections.Demographics: As of the 2025 census, Maltese-born natives make up the majority, numbering 574,348 out of a total population of 588,254. All in all, 89.1 percent are Caucasian; 5.2 percent Asian; 1.7 percent Arabian; 1.5 percent African; 1.3 percent Hispanic; and 1.2 percent a mix between two or more of these ethnicities. The majority of Malta is ethnically Maltese, which is considered as a mix of various ethnicities.
sections.Religion:
The predominant religion in Malta is Catholicism, established in the second article of the Constitution of Malta as the state religion, and it is also reflected in various elements of Maltese culture, although there are entrenched provisions for the freedom of religion.

In a survey by Malta Today, the overwhelming majority of the Maltese population adheres to Christianity (95.2 percent), with Catholicism the main denomination at 93.9 percent. 4.5 percent of the population declared themselves either atheist or agnostic, one of Europe's lowest figures. According to a Eurobarometer survey in 2019, 83 percent of the population identified as Catholic.
sections.Languages: Maltese (Maltese: Malti) is a Semitic language which holds close ties to both Arabic and Sicilian. The Maltese alphabet consists of 30 letters based on the Latin alphabet. Maltese is one of the two constitutional languages of Malta and is considered the national language. The second official language is English, and hence laws are enacted both in Maltese and English. However, Article 74 of the Constitution states that "if there is any conflict between the Maltese and the English texts of any law, the Maltese text shall prevail." Many speakers of English use a local dialect, Maltese English. Maltese Sign Language is also used in the country.
sections.Cuisine:
Maltese cuisine has been strongly influenced by Sicilian and Italian cuisine, along with food from Africa and Arabia. Food has been historically important in the development of a national identity, in particular the traditional fenkata (the eating of stewed or fried rabbit). Potatoes are also Maltese staples. Maltese restaurants have also earned multiple awards, with Malta having six Michelin starred and 23 Michelin plated cookeries.

A variety of grapes is common in Malta, including Girgentina and Ġellewża. There is a large wine industry, with significant production using these native grapes. A number of wines have achieved Protected Designation of Origin with wines produced from grapes cultivated in Malta and Gozo designated as "DOK" wines (Denominazzjoni ta' l-Oriġini Kontrollata). Although beer is not a popular beverage in Malta, there is a common one called Cisk.
sections.Sport:
Football is one of Malta's most popular sports. Other popular sports include boċċi, horse racing, gostra, regatta, water polo, clay pigeon shooting, and motorsports.

Fifty percent of people in Malta follow football. The most popular football team in Malta is Valletta F.C., with 15 percent support.

In 2018, Malta hosted its first Esports tournament, "Supernova CS:GO Malta", a Counter-Strike: Global Offensive tournament, and became the primary location for hosting the ESL Pro League.
sections.Music: Although Maltese music today is largely Western, traditional Maltese music includes what is known as għana, which sometimes consists of background folk guitar music while a few people, generally men, take turns to argue a point in a sing-song voice. Since 1960, the Malta Song Festival has been organised annually. Traditional instruments include the Żaqq, a bagpipe associated with Christmas.
